q: The lock-in period in the case of a term deposit means that
explain: Lock-in is the period during which the deposit cannot be withdrawn early; it has nothing to do with lockers or other accounts.

q: A deposit that can be withdrawn without any advance notice is called a
explain: Demand deposits can be withdrawn at any time; time deposits are locked for a fixed period.

q: Which type of account has no minimum or average balance requirement?
explain: A zero-balance account does not require the holder to keep a minimum or average balance.

q: A negotiable instrument issued by a bank in exchange for funds deposited with it, usually bearing interest, is a
explain: A CD is a negotiable instrument issued against deposited funds for a fixed period.

q: From a banking perspective, a contract that guarantees income or returns in exchange for a large lump sum or periodic payments is a(n)
explain: Annuities are contracts that promise income or returns against money deposited as a lump sum or in periodic payments.

q: A card signed by each depositor, used as a means of identification and representing a contract between bank and depositor, is called a
explain: The signature card is the specimen-signature record that forms a contract between bank and depositor.

q: The bank service in which securities and valuables are protected in the bank's vaults is called
explain: Safekeeping means the bank holds securities and valuables securely for its customers.

q: A payment that is electronically deposited into an individual's account is known as
explain: Salary and benefit credits sent electronically are direct deposits.

q: The balance of an account after subtracting holds, uncollected funds and restrictions is the
explain: Available balance is what the customer can actually withdraw.

q: After the bank's cut-off time, a deposit is considered received
options: only after the cheque is cleared by the RBI
explain: A deposit made after the cut-off time is treated as received on the next banking day.

q: Available credit on a credit card account is
options: the credit limit minus the present balance
the present balance minus the credit limit
the total of all past payments
explain: Available credit is the headroom left under the limit.

q: Cash deposits, or cheques for which payment has been received, are known as
explain: Collected funds are those for which payment has actually been received.

q: A cheque that a bank refuses to pay because of insufficient funds or a signature mismatch is called a
explain: A bounced (dishonoured) cheque is one the bank refuses to pay for a valid reason.

q: A cheque written by a depositor that has not yet been presented for payment is called a(n)
explain: Outstanding cheques are issued but yet to be presented or paid.

q: A cheque drawn on a bank and signed by an authorised bank official is also known as a
explain: An official cheque is the same as a cashier's cheque.

q: An order not to pay a cheque that has been issued but not yet cashed is called
explain: A stop payment instruction prevents the bank from paying the cheque; banks usually charge a fee.

q: According to the study material, a stale-dated cheque is one presented
options: 180 days (6 months) or more after the issue date
on the same day as issue
explain: Stale-dated cheques are presented too long after issue and can be returned unpaid.

q: Fraudulent signing or alteration of another person's name on an instrument such as a cheque is called
explain: Forgery means signing or altering an instrument to deceive or defraud.

q: In cheque clearing, the amount is
options: credited to the issuer and debited from the beneficiary
debited from the issuer's account and credited to the beneficiary's account
held by the clearing house permanently
explain: The clearing house settles the cheque by debiting the issuer and crediting the beneficiary.

q: Which process uses the cheque number, account number and bank identifier from a cheque to make a one-time electronic payment?
explain: In electronic cheque conversion, the cheque itself is not the method of payment; its details trigger an electronic transfer.

q: Assets offered to secure a loan, which can be seized on default, are called
explain: Collateral secures a loan; on default it becomes subject to seizure.

q: An agency that collects individuals' credit information and sells it to creditors is a
explain: Credit bureaus supply credit reports to banks and other lenders.

q: A pre-approved loan authorisation with a borrowing limit based on creditworthiness, allowing several loans without reapplying, is a
explain: Within the limit, a borrower can draw repeatedly without a new application.

q: The ratio of the loan principal to the appraised value of the asset is called the
explain: LTV compares the amount borrowed with the appraised value of the asset.

q: A debt that was not paid when due is termed
explain: Delinquency is a missed due payment; a deferred payment is postponed by agreement.

q: A penalty charged to a borrower for repaying a loan before its due date is a
explain: Prepayment penalty applies to early repayment; a late charge applies to delayed repayment.

q: A credit agreement, typically a credit card, that lets a customer borrow against a pre-approved limit and be billed only for the amount borrowed is
explain: Revolving credit is also called open-end credit or a charge account.

q: Which of the following is a number roughly between 300 and 800 that measures a person's creditworthiness, as per the study material?
explain: The score summarises a credit report into a single number.

q: In a mortgage, the borrower is called the
explain: Mortgagor = borrower; mortgagee = lender.

q: In a mortgage, the lender is called the
explain: The mortgagee is the lender who holds the property as security.

q: A legal process by which property that secures a defaulted loan may be sold to repay the loan is called
explain: Foreclosure lets the lender sell the collateral property after default.

q: A bank's legal right to seize funds a debtor or guarantor holds on deposit to cover a loan in default is the right of
explain: Right of offset lets a bank adjust a defaulted loan against the borrower's deposits.

q: When more money is withdrawn from an account than is available in it, the excess is called
explain: The account is then said to be overdrawn.

q: A home equity loan is a loan against
options: the entire market value of the home
the difference between the home's selling value and the amount still owed
explain: It lets homeowners tap the equity built up in their home; it is often called a second mortgage.

q: The rate at which the RBI lends funds to commercial banks, usually a long-term loan, is the
explain: The Bank Rate is the RBI's long-term lending rate; the repo rate is for short-term borrowing against securities.

q: The rate at which a bank borrows money from the RBI by pledging government securities is the
explain: Repo = repurchase rate: banks sell or pledge securities to the RBI.

q: The rate offered by the RBI when banks deposit surplus funds with it for short periods is the
explain: Reverse repo absorbs liquidity from banks.

q: The minimum interest rate of a bank below which it cannot lend (except in RBI-allowed cases) is the
explain: The Base Rate is each bank's own floor rate; exceptions include DRI advances and loans to staff.

q: BPLR stands for
explain: BPLR mainly applied to loans sanctioned before the Base Rate system began in July 2010.

q: Interest that has been earned or accumulated but not yet paid is called
explain: Accrued interest is also termed interest receivable.

q: Banks borrow money from the RBI at which of the following rates?
explain: Banks borrow at the repo rate and park surplus at the reverse repo rate. SLR and CRR are ratios, not rates.

q: Reverse repo means
options: injecting liquidity into the market by buying government securities
absorption of liquidity from the market by sale of government securities
lending money to commercial banks at the bank rate
explain: In a reverse repo the RBI takes funds from banks, absorbing liquidity.

q: The time interval between the dates on which regular periodic statements are issued is the
explain: The billing cycle is the gap between two statement dates.

q: A four-character secret number given to cardholders to prevent unauthorised use is called a
explain: PIN stands for Personal Identification Number.

q: The location where a transaction takes place, including systems that transfer funds at retail outlets, is called
explain: POS stands for Point of Sale.

q: The full form of ACH in banking is
explain: ACH is an electronic clearing facility for credits and debits between banks.

q: A bank's commitment, issued on behalf of a buyer, to pay a seller a specific amount on meeting stated conditions is a
explain: LoCs are widely used in international trade, where the seller must submit required documents.

q: IFSC is a code of how many characters?
explain: IFSC (Indian Financial System Code) has 11 characters and identifies branches for NEFT and RTGS.

q: The MICR code that identifies a bank branch is a
explain: MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) is a 9-digit code printed on cheques.

q: SWIFT stands for
options: System for Wire Interbank Financial Transactions
Society for World Investment and Finance Trade
Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication
explain: SWIFT codes support international bank-to-bank transfers.

q: A SWIFT code is made up of
explain: The structure is 4 (bank) + 2 (country) + 2 (location) + optional 3 (branch).

q: In an 11-character SWIFT code, the last three characters represent the
explain: The optional branch code is the last 3 characters; an 8-character code refers to the primary office.

q: India was which nation to join the SWIFT network?
explain: India was the 74th nation to join SWIFT.

q: Underwriting new issues, accepting trade bills and advising on mergers and acquisitions together are known as
explain: Merchant banking is a bundle of financial services for customers.

q: Banking services provided to corporate entities, large institutions and other financial institutions are called
explain: Wholesale banking caters to big institutional clients.

q: A company that invests its clients' pooled funds into securities matching its declared objectives, earning through service fees, is
explain: Mutual funds, hedge funds and pension plans are run by asset management companies.

q: A company which pools money from investors and invests in stocks, bonds and shares is called a
explain: A mutual fund collects money from many investors and invests it in securities.

q: The Association of National Exchange Members of India (ANMI) is a body of
options: brokers operating in the national exchanges
explain: ANMI represents brokers of the national stock exchanges.

q: Creating the appearance that money obtained from serious crimes such as drug trafficking came from a legitimate source is called
explain: Money laundering disguises illegal proceeds as legitimate funds.

q: GAAR stands for
explain: GAAR is a set of rules to check tax avoidance.

q: The RBI introduced Know Your Customer (KYC) guidelines for all banks in
explain: KYC was introduced in 2002; banks had to be fully compliant by 31 December 2005.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four key elements of a bank's KYC policy?
explain: The four elements are acceptance policy, identification procedures, transaction monitoring and risk management.

q: When was the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority of India (PFRDA) established?
explain: PFRDA was set up on 23 August 2003 and is headquartered in New Delhi.

q: PFRDA regulates the National Pension System and also administers which scheme?
explain: PFRDA administers the Atal Pension Yojana (APY).

q: Consider the statements about Non-Fungible Tokens. 1: They can digitally represent physical assets. 2: They are unique cryptographic tokens on a blockchain. 3: They can be exchanged at equivalency and so serve as a medium of commercial transactions. Which are correct?
explain: NFTs are unique, so they are not exchanged at equivalency and cannot serve as a common medium of exchange; statement 3 is wrong.

q: What term is used for the maximum capital that a company can raise in its lifetime?
explain: Authorised (registered or nominal) capital is the ceiling set in the company's documents.

q: Zero-based budgeting (ZBB) means that
options: the budget is a fixed percentage of sales
each year, budgeting starts from scratch
the budget is always kept at zero
explain: ZBB requires every item to be justified afresh rather than carried over from last year.

q: For buying and selling precious metals such as gold and silver, the market is called the
explain: Bullion refers to precious metals traded in bulk.

q: Which measure of fiscal reform has the Government of India adopted?
options: Fixing a higher rate of growth
Bringing down the fiscal deficit to a particular level by an Act of law
Allocating more funds to job-oriented schemes
Allocating more funds for education of 6-14 year olds
explain: Fiscal deficit targets are set by law (the FRBM framework), which is a fiscal reform measure.

q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a type of inflation?
explain: Deflationary inflation does not exist; the listed types include wage, price power, cost-push, sectoral, stagflation, mild and hyper.

q: Which of the following is a negative effect of inflation?
options: It increases the real value of money
It raises the real burden of debt
explain: Inflation lowers the real value of money and discourages savings.

q: Liquidity means
options: how cash is converted into gold
how uncertain money market conditions are
how easily and quickly an asset can be converted into other assets
how cash is converted into SDRs
explain: Liquidity is the ease and speed of conversion.

q: The liquidity risk of a firm tells about its
options: ability to satisfy all future obligations
explain: Liquidity risk concerns whether the firm can meet its obligations when due.

q: If the cash reserve ratio is lowered by the RBI, its impact on credit creation will be to
explain: A lower CRR leaves banks with more lendable funds, so credit creation rises.
